title: Small bands today, the Condon chapter and rock and roll
summary: Young bands now play the old style; Souchon urges recording the old Negro musicians, who are not being succeeded, and criticises rock and roll.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Since the... The Bible of the... Small bands, what about the use of them at private parties?
Well, I think you find that more and more now.
Not only the, uh... Union bands, both Negro and white, but there's any number of young bands that are coming up. And that's one of the things...
They play the old... Oh, yeah.

As close as they can. Uh... One of the points that I brought up, and I wrote a chapter for Eddie Condon's book that's coming out soon. Uh... It's an evaluation of the situation of jazz music in New Orleans. And the point I made was that they'd better record these old Negro musicians as much as they can, because as soon as this generation is gone, the Negro jazz is gone. The younger Negroes want to get away from jazz as far as they can, because it smacks of Jim Crow and of slavery and its origins, African origins, they want to forget. And so any of them that, uh, uh, do play at all now will not play the jazz idiom. They'll try to learn progressive, uh, those that don't have that much education, because I do think that kind of music takes a great deal of knowledge. They, uh, they'll play rock and roll, which will be dead damn soon, I hope. It's, uh, incidentally, my opinion on that, uh, if you'll forgive me for flinging it around, it's a very bad combination of hillbilly and blues, race records. It's neither one or the other, and it's not good. The, uh, I think the reason it's caught on with the younger generation, because they've gotten away from complex tunes that, uh, are hard to remember, both the melody and the harmonies and the words, and they've gotten back to a very simple pattern that anyone can remember.
